Quote of the day

"If you live 5 minutes away from Bill Gates, I bet you are rich."

The quote is the whole idea of this session. To guess something about you, look at the people who live closest to you. That is K-nearest neighbours.

K-nearest neighbours, explained

Classification: predicting a category

In sessions 2 to 6, most of what we predicted was a number: a wage, a volume of exports, a price. Today the outcome is a category: Up or Down, crisis or no crisis, red or green. Predicting a category is called classification, and a model that does it is a classifier.

A classifier is judged by its mistakes. We count how often its prediction \(\hat y_i\) differs from the truth \(y_i\):

  • The training error rate is the share of mistakes on the observations used to fit the model:

\[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} I(y_i \neq \hat y_i)\]

where \(I(y_i \neq \hat y_i)\) is 1 if observation \(i\) is misclassified and 0 otherwise. So the formula simply counts the mistakes and divides by \(n\).

  • The test error rate is the same share, computed on observations the model has not seen: \(\text{Ave}\big(I(y_0 \neq \hat y_0)\big)\)

Keep this distinction in mind for the whole session. The training error tells us how well the model remembers the past. The test error tells us how well it will do on new cases, and that is the only one we care about.

The idea: tell me who your neighbours are

  • In words
  • In symbols

KNN has no equation, no coefficients and no theory of how the data were produced. It rests on one intuition: observations that look alike tend to belong to the same class.

To classify a new observation, KNN does three things:

  1. It measures the distance between the new observation and every observation in the training data.
  2. It keeps the \(K\) closest ones, its “nearest neighbours”. \(K\) is a number we choose: 1, 3, 25, …
  3. It lets them vote. The new observation gets the class that most of its neighbours have.

That is the whole algorithm. Everything else in this session is about two questions: how to measure “close”, and how many neighbours to ask.

Given a positive integer \(K\) and a new observation \(x_0\), KNN finds the \(K\) training points closest to \(x_0\) (call that set \(N_0\)). It estimates the probability of each class \(j\) as the share of the neighbours that belong to it:

\[\widehat{\Pr}(Y = j \mid X = x_0) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i \in N_0} I(y_i = j)\]

Then \(x_0\) goes to the class with the largest share.

Read the formula out loud: “among my \(K\) neighbours, count those of class \(j\), and divide by \(K\).” With \(K = 5\) and three blue neighbours, \(\widehat{\Pr}(\text{blue}) = 3/5 = 0.6\), so the prediction is blue.

KNN with K = 3, in a picture

  • Left. We want to classify the black cross, with \(K = 3\). KNN finds the three closest observations (the circle): two blue, one orange. So \(\widehat{\Pr}(\text{blue}) = 2/3\), \(\widehat{\Pr}(\text{orange}) = 1/3\), and the cross is predicted blue.
  • Right. Now do the same vote at every point of the plane. Where blue wins, the plane is shaded blue; where orange wins, orange. The line between the two colours is the \(K = 3\) decision boundary: on one side of it, KNN says blue; on the other, orange.

KNN by hand: you are the algorithm

Before a computer does it, we do it ourselves, with a pencil. Six observations, one new point, and the three steps of KNN: distance, nearest, vote.

  • The data
  • The distances

A training set of six observations, three predictors and one qualitative response.

We want to predict \(Y\) for the test point \(X_1 = X_2 = X_3 = 0\) using \(K\)-nearest neighbours.

First step: compute the Euclidean distance between each observation and the test point:

\[d(a, b) = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p} (a_j - b_j)^2}\]

With \(b = (0, 0, 0)\) this is just \(\sqrt{X_1^2 + X_2^2 + X_3^2}\).

Obs. \(X_1\) \(X_2\) \(X_3\) \(Y\)
1 0 3 0 Red
2 2 0 0 Red
3 0 1 3 Red
4 0 1 2 Green
5 −1 0 1 Green
6 1 1 1 Red
Obs. \(X_1\) \(X_2\) \(X_3\) \(Y\) \(d\) to \((0,0,0)\)
1 0 3 0 Red \(\sqrt{9} = 3.000\)
2 2 0 0 Red \(\sqrt{4} = 2.000\)
3 0 1 3 Red \(\sqrt{10} = 3.162\)
4 0 1 2 Green \(\sqrt{5} = 2.236\)
5 −1 0 1 Green \(\sqrt{2} = 1.414\)
6 1 1 1 Red \(\sqrt{3} = 1.732\)

The same, in Python:

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# The six observations, and their colour
by_hand = pd.DataFrame({
    "X1": [0, 2, 0, 0, -1, 1],
    "X2": [3, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1],
    "X3": [0, 0, 3, 2, 1, 1],
    "Y":  ["Red", "Red", "Red", "Green", "Green", "Red"],
}, index=[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])

# Distance to the test point (0, 0, 0)
by_hand["distance"] = np.sqrt(
    by_hand["X1"]**2 + by_hand["X2"]**2 + by_hand["X3"]**2)

# Nearest first
by_hand = by_hand.sort_values("distance")
print(by_hand.round(3))

2   2   0   0    Red     2.000

1   0   3   0    Red     3.000
3   0   1   3    Red     3.162

print("K = 1 predicts:", by_hand["Y"].iloc[:1].mode()[0])
print("K = 3 predicts:", by_hand["Y"].iloc[:3].mode()[0])
K = 1 predicts: Green
K = 3 predicts: Red

The choice of K: how many neighbours?

  • \(K = 1\): each point is classified by its single nearest neighbour. The boundary wraps around every stray blue point in orange territory, and every stray orange point in blue. The training error is 0, because every point is its own nearest neighbour, yet on new points it makes 16% mistakes. Low bias, high variance: the model believes every detail of the sample, including the noise.
  • \(K = 11\): the boundary follows the true one (purple, dashed) closely, and the test error, 12%, is about the best any rule can do on these data. KNN knows nothing about how the data were generated, yet it finds the shape.
  • \(K = 100\): half the data votes on every point, so the boundary is almost a straight line and misses the bend of the true boundary. High bias, low variance: the model is stable, but too simple.

Bias and variance, in three pictures

What we just saw with \(K\) is a general law of statistical learning, the bias–variance trade-off. A rigid model is wrong in the same way every time (bias). A flexible model is right on average but changes a lot from one sample to the next (variance). The best model sits in between.

Training error is not test error

With \(K = 1\) the training error is 0, but the test error is not. In general, as a classifier becomes more flexible, its training error keeps falling, while its test error first falls and then rises again.

The figure plots both as flexibility, \(1/K\), increases: training error in blue (on the 200 observations used to fit), test error in orange (on 5,000 new observations). The dashed line is the lowest error any rule could reach, because the two classes overlap.

Choosing the level of flexibility is the whole game. The U-shape of the test error is what makes it hard: the training error always says “more flexible”, and it is wrong.

A nonlinear boundary: large K or small?

If the true decision boundary in this problem is highly nonlinear, would we expect the best value for \(K\) to be large or small? Why?

Small. A small \(K\) is flexible: the boundary is drawn by a few nearby points, so it can bend wherever the true boundary bends. A large \(K\) averages over many points, which smooths the boundary towards a straight line — exactly what a highly nonlinear problem cannot afford. (Too small, though, and it bends around noise: that is the \(K = 1\) picture.)

Watch a decision boundary being built

Everything in this section — a boundary, a class region, the cost of flexibility — can be watched happening, in a browser, in about four minutes.

playground.tensorflow.org — the link is pre-set to the exercise below. Press the play button.

The problem is two concentric rings, and the inputs are only \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) — the raw coordinates, nothing engineered.

It is a neural network rather than anything this course fits, and that does not matter here. What is on screen is a decision boundary and a test error, which are the two objects of this session.

Four things to try, and what each one shows

1 · Remove both hidden layers, leaving the inputs wired straight to the output. Run it. The boundary is a straight line, and it cannot separate a ring from its centre — the error stalls near 0.5. This is the limit that made session 4’s logistic regression a line, and it is why we need something else.

2 · Put the layers back and run it again. A closed curve forms. Nothing told it to draw a circle; the hidden units composed one out of straight pieces. That is what “flexible” buys you.

3 · Now add capacity — eight neurons in each of four layers. Watch the two loss numbers separate: training loss keeps falling while test loss turns upward, and the boundary starts bulging toward individual points. You are watching variance, live. It is the same curve as \(K\) getting too small, a few slides back.

4 · Reset, and instead tick the \(X_1^2\) and \(X_2^2\) input features. Now even no hidden layer separates the rings almost perfectly — because \(X_1^2 + X_2^2\) is the radius, and in that coordinate the problem was always linear.

What step 4 was really about

You can buy the non-linearity with model flexibility, or with a feature you thought of yourself. They are substitutes.

The second is cheaper, more stable and easier to defend — when you can think of the feature. Knowing that \(X_1^2 + X_2^2\) is a radius is subject knowledge, not statistics, and it is the part a model cannot supply for you.

Which is the session’s argument in one sentence: complexity is what you spend when understanding runs out. Session 5 penalised that spending; session 6 wrote the non-linearity in by hand as a quadratic; this session measures what it costs when you cannot.

Cross-validation: why it is magical

The question every model must answer

How well will this model do on data it has never seen?

The classical approach (sessions 2 to 6). We fitted a model on all the data, then judged it on that same data: the \(R^2\), the \(t\)-statistics, the \(p\)-values, the standard errors.

Those numbers describe how well the model fits the sample. To say anything about new data, they lean on assumptions: the model is correctly specified, the errors are normal and independent, and so on. If the assumptions fail, the numbers can mislead, and nothing in them warns us.

The problem with flexible models. A flexible model can always fit the sample better. KNN with \(K = 1\) has a training error of 0. A polynomial of degree 20 has an \(R^2\) close to 1. In-sample fit rewards exactly the models that will predict worst.

What we really want is the error on new data, the out-of-sample error. But new data have not arrived yet, and the test set may be used only once, at the very end.

So we need to estimate the out-of-sample error from the data we already have. That is what cross-validation does.

Train, validate, test: three words to know

Every machine-learning project cuts its data into parts, and gives each part one job. The three words below come back in every course, paper and piece of code on the subject.

What it is What it is used for In the stock-market example
Training set The observations the model learns from Fitting the model. For KNN, the neighbours are looked for here The days of 2001–2004
Validation set Observations hidden from the fit, but taken from the training data Choosing a setting, such as \(K\): the setting with the fewest mistakes on it wins Each round’s hidden block, in cross-validation
Test set Observations kept locked away until everything is decided Judging the final model, once, as if it were new data The days of 2005

Cross-validation is a way to get a validation set without losing training data: it cuts the training data into folds and lets each fold play “validation” in turn. So the validation set is not a fixed part of the data, but a role that moves.

The golden rule: the test set must never help to choose anything. Once you change the model because of its test score, the test set has become a validation set, and you no longer have an honest measure of how well the model predicts.

The power of sampling

The trick is simple and powerful: if we cannot get new data, we manufacture some from our own sample. Hide part of the data, fit the model on the rest, and test it on the hidden part. For the model, the hidden part is new data. Then do it again with a different part hidden, and again.

Cut the training data into \(k\) folds. Fit on \(k - 1\) of them, count the mistakes on the one left out, rotate, and average:

\[\text{CV}_{(k)} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k} \text{Err}_i, \qquad \text{Err}_i = \frac{1}{n_i}\sum_{j \in \text{fold } i} I(y_j \neq \hat y_j)\]

\(k = 5\) or \(k = 10\) are the usual choices. Every observation is used to fit the model \(k - 1\) times and to test it exactly once. With \(k = n\), each observation is left out on its own: leave-one-out cross-validation.

Classical fit against cross-validation

Classical, in-sample Cross-validation, out-of-sample
The question it answers How well does the model describe this sample? How well will it predict a new observation?
What it needs A formula for the model, and assumptions about the errors Only that new data look like the data we have
Which models it works for Those with a theory: OLS, logit, … Any model: KNN, trees, forests, networks, …
What it does with a more flexible model Rewards it: fit always improves Penalises it as soon as it starts fitting noise
What it says about uncertainty A standard error, if the assumptions hold \(k\) errors: their spread shows how stable the result is

The two are not enemies. Cross-validation does not replace the coefficients and \(p\)-values of an explanatory model. It answers a different question, the one that matters when the goal is to predict.

Why it is magical

  1. It needs no theory. No formula for the variance, no assumption on the errors. One idea, sampling, replaces pages of mathematics.
  2. It tunes anything. \(K\) in KNN, \(\lambda\) in ridge and lasso (session 5), the depth of a tree, the size of a neural network: the same loop chooses them all.
  3. It referees between models. KNN against a logit against a random forest, each scored on data it did not see, on equal terms.
  4. It uses every observation twice, once to fit and once to check. That matters when data are scarce, as they usually are in international business.
  5. It tells you how sure to be. It gives \(k\) errors, not one. If two models differ by less than the spread of those errors, the difference may be noise.

Three rules, or it lies. (1) Everything learned from data, such as standardising, happens inside each fold: that is what the Pipeline does in the code. (2) With time series, the folds respect time: never fit on the future to predict the past. (3) Cross-validation chooses; the test set judges, once, at the very end.

A financial example: can KNN predict the stock market?

The question, and the plan

Can the market’s returns of the last two days tell us whether it will go up or down today?

We will answer the way a data scientist at a bank would. The work is split into two files, because in real life the two jobs happen at different times:

File 1 · session08_1_train.py — the laboratory. It loads five years of data, chooses \(K\) by cross-validation, judges the model once on a year it never saw, and saves the trained model in a file.

File 2 · session08_2_predict.py — the trading desk. No data to download, no training. It loads the saved model and predicts one new date: a genuine out-of-sample prediction.

  • Save both files in one folder of your own, open that folder in VS Codium, run File 1, then File 2.
  • Once, in the VS Codium terminal: pip install pandas numpy matplotlib scikit-learn

macOS, Python from python.org: if reading the data fails with CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED, run its certificate installer once, then try again: open /Applications/Python\ 3*/Install\ Certificates.command

The slides that follow show the two files step by step, with their output. In a .py file a result only appears if you print() it, which is why every step prints what it wants you to see.

The workflow, and how a classifier is scored

  • Eight steps, two files
  • What KNN needs
  • Confusion matrix
  • Reading it
  • Pre-processing

File 1, the laboratory

  1. Load the data and look at it
  2. Put the newest day aside: it plays “tomorrow” for File 2
  3. Split by time: learn from 2001–2004, test on 2005
  4. Cut the training years into folds, in time order
  5. Cross-validate by hand, for one \(K\), to see the loop
  6. Cross-validate every \(K\) at once, and keep the best
  7. Open the test year, once, and judge the chosen model
  8. Refit on all the history, and save the model

File 2, the trading desk: load the model, predict one new date.

  1. The predictors of the training data — X_train below
  2. The class labels of the training data — y_train (Up / Down)
  3. The predictors of the data to predict — X_test
  4. A value for \(K\), the number of neighbours — chosen by cross-validation

From the four cells of the confusion matrix:

\[\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + FP + TN + FN}\]

\[\text{Recall (sensitivity, TPR)} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} \qquad \text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}\]

\[\text{Specificity} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP} \qquad \text{False positive rate} = 1 - \text{Specificity} = \frac{FP}{TN + FP}\]

\[F_1 = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN} = \frac{2 \times \text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}\]

KNN measures distances, so a predictor in large units would dominate one in small units. Put them on the same scale first:

\[\text{Normalisation: } x_{\text{normalised}} = \frac{x - x_{\min}}{x_{\max} - x_{\min}} \qquad \text{Standardisation: } x_{\text{standardised}} = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\]

In scikit-learn, standardisation is StandardScaler().

File 1 · Step 1: the data

Smarket: the S&P 500 index, every trading day from 2001 to 2005, from the textbook An Introduction to Statistical Learning. Each row is one day. We want to predict its Direction from the returns of the days before.

  • Data collection
  • Data description
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Smarket: 1,250 trading days of the S&P 500, 2001-2005 (ISLR textbook data)
URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/intro-stat-learning/ISLP/main/ISLP/data/Smarket.csv"
smarket = pd.read_csv(URL)

print(smarket.shape)                         # (rows, columns)
print(smarket.head())
print(smarket["Direction"].value_counts())   # how many Up days, how many Down

1,250 trading days, 9 variables. We give KNN only Lag1 and Lag2, the returns of the last two days.

Variable Description
Year The year of the observation
Lag1 % return of the market the previous day
Lag2 % return two days before
Lag3 … Lag5 % return three to five days before
Volume Shares traded (billions)
Today % return that day
Direction Up or Down: did the market rise that day? — the label

Today is the answer in disguise (Direction is just its sign), so it must never be a predictor.

File 1 · Steps 2–3: one day aside, then a split by time

Two decisions before any model is fitted, and both protect us from fooling ourselves.

  • Step 2. We hide the very last day in the data, 30 December 2005. File 1 never sees it. File 2 will predict it, as if it were tomorrow.
  • Step 3. We split the rest by time: the model learns from 2001–2004 and is judged on 2005. Never shuffle a time series. A random split would put days of 2005 in the training data, and the model would learn from the future to “predict” the past: its score would be too good to be true.
# Step 2 · Put the newest day aside: File 2 will predict it
new_day = smarket.tail(1)                     # 30 December 2005
history = smarket.iloc[:-1]                   # every day except the last one
print(new_day[["Year", "Lag1", "Lag2", "Direction"]])

# Step 3 · Split by time: learn from 2001-2004, test on 2005
predictors = ["Lag1", "Lag2"]                 # the returns of the last two days
train = history[history["Year"] < 2005]
test = history[history["Year"] == 2005]
X_train, y_train = train[predictors], train["Direction"]
X_test, y_test = test[predictors], test["Direction"]

print(f"training set: {len(train)} days (2001-2004)  <- used to learn and to choose K")
print(f"test set:     {len(test)} days (2005)       <- locked away until Step 7")
      Year   Lag1  Lag2 Direction
1249  2005 -0.298  0.13      Down
training set: 998 days (2001-2004)  <- used to learn and to choose K
test set:     251 days (2005)       <- locked away until Step 7

File 1 · Step 4: cross-validation folds, in time order

We must choose \(K\) without touching 2005. Cross-validation does it inside the training years. But this is a time series, so the standard folds would break rule (2): they would fit on 2004 to predict 2002. Instead, each round fits on everything up to a date, and validates on the block that comes next.

from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit

folds = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)           # 6 blocks in time order, 5 rounds
for r, (fit_rows, check_rows) in enumerate(folds.split(X_train), start=1):
    print(f"round {r}: fit on days 1 to {fit_rows[-1] + 1}, "
          f"validate on days {check_rows[0] + 1} to {check_rows[-1] + 1}")
round 1: fit on days 1 to 168, validate on days 169 to 334
round 2: fit on days 1 to 334, validate on days 335 to 500
round 3: fit on days 1 to 500, validate on days 501 to 666
round 4: fit on days 1 to 666, validate on days 667 to 832
round 5: fit on days 1 to 832, validate on days 833 to 998

File 1 · Step 5: cross-validation by hand, for one K

Before letting scikit-learn do it for us, we do it once by hand, for \(K = 25\), to see that there is no magic inside, only a loop.

import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Standardise, then KNN, glued into ONE model: the scaler is refitted with
# the model each time, on the fitting rows only, so it never peeks at the hidden block.
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=25))

errors = []
for r, (fit_rows, check_rows) in enumerate(folds.split(X_train), start=1):
    model.fit(X_train.iloc[fit_rows], y_train.iloc[fit_rows])          # learn
    accuracy = model.score(X_train.iloc[check_rows], y_train.iloc[check_rows])  # test on the hidden block
    errors.append(1 - accuracy)
    print(f"round {r}: error on the hidden block = {1 - accuracy:.3f}")

print(f"K = 25: cross-validated error = {np.mean(errors):.3f}")
round 1: error on the hidden block = 0.524
round 2: error on the hidden block = 0.518
round 3: error on the hidden block = 0.446
round 4: error on the hidden block = 0.548
round 5: error on the hidden block = 0.494
K = 25: cross-validated error = 0.506

The five rounds do not agree exactly, and that spread is information: it says how much the error of one \(K\) moves from one period to the next. The average is our estimate of how \(K = 25\) would do on days it has not seen. Why the scaler? KNN measures distances, so a predictor in large units would outvote one in small units. StandardScaler puts every column on the same scale, \((x - \mu)/\sigma\).

File 1 · Step 6: cross-validation for every K at once

  • Code
  • The curve
  • Reading it

GridSearchCV is exactly the loop of Step 5, run for every \(K\) in a list. It keeps the \(K\) with the best cross-validated accuracy, and refits the model with it on all the training days.

from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

# K = 1, 3, 5, ..., 151: odd numbers, so a two-class vote can never tie.
# "kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors" = inside the pipeline, the KNN step's n_neighbors.
k_values = list(range(1, 152, 2))
search = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier()),
                      {"kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors": k_values},
                      cv=folds)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)

best_k = search.best_params_["kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors"]
majority = y_train.value_counts(normalize=True).max()   # share of the commonest class
print(f"best K = {best_k}")
print(f"cross-validated accuracy at that K = {search.best_score_:.3f}")
print(f"always predicting the commonest direction = {majority:.3f}   <- the bar to beat")
best K = 85
cross-validated accuracy at that K = 0.525
always predicting the commonest direction = 0.508   <- the bar to beat
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 3))
plt.plot(k_values, search.cv_results_["mean_test_score"], "o-", markersize=3,
         label="KNN, cross-validated accuracy")
plt.axhline(majority, color="red", linestyle="--", label="always predict the commonest direction")
plt.axvline(best_k, color="grey", linestyle=":", label=f"chosen K = {best_k}")
plt.xlabel("K (number of neighbours)")
plt.ylabel("accuracy on the hidden blocks")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
  • Small \(K\) (left): flexible, low bias, high variance. The boundary follows single days, and the accuracy jumps around.
  • Large \(K\) (right): rigid, high bias, low variance. The prediction flattens towards “the market usually goes up”.
  • The chosen \(K\) is the best compromise on hidden blocks, not on the data used to fit. Notice how small the gain over the red line is: we already suspect that the last two days say little about today.

File 1 · Step 7: open the test year, once

\(K\) is chosen. Only now do we look at 2005, and we do it once. If we went back and changed \(K\) after seeing this score, 2005 would have become training data, and the score would no longer be honest.

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

y_pred = search.predict(X_test)

# Rows = what really happened, columns = what the model said
table = pd.DataFrame(confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred, labels=["Down", "Up"]),
                     index=["actual Down", "actual Up"],
                     columns=["predicted Down", "predicted Up"])
print(table)

accuracy = (y_pred == y_test).mean()
baseline = y_test.value_counts(normalize=True).max()
print(f"KNN accuracy on 2005:                      {accuracy:.3f}")
print(f"always predicting the commonest direction: {baseline:.3f}")
             predicted Down  predicted Up
actual Down              45            65
actual Up                59            82
KNN accuracy on 2005:                      0.506
always predicting the commonest direction: 0.562

Read this honestly. KNN does not beat the simple rule “the market goes up”. The last two days’ returns carry almost no usable signal about today. That is a finding, not a failure: if markets were easy to predict from yesterday, traders would exploit it until they were not. Cross-validation and the test year told us the truth before we bet any money.

File 1 · Step 8: refit on all the history, and save

The test year has done its job: it gave us an honest score. Before using the model, we let it learn from everything we know, 2001 to 2005 except the day kept aside, with the \(K\) that cross-validation chose. Then we save it in a file, so that File 2 can use it without training again.

import joblib                      # installed together with scikit-learn: saves a model to a file

final_model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=best_k))
final_model.fit(history[predictors], history["Direction"])

joblib.dump(final_model, "knn_smarket.joblib")
print(f"Saved: knn_smarket.joblib  (KNN with K = {best_k}, learned from {len(history)} days)")
Saved: knn_smarket.joblib  (KNN with K = 85, learned from 1249 days)

The file holds the whole pipeline: the scaler with the means and standard deviations it learned, the chosen \(K\), and the days among which KNN will look for neighbours.

File 2: predict one new date

A new morning: 30 December 2005. The model has never seen this day. All we know is what the market did on the two days before: it fell 0.298% on 29 December, and rose 0.130% on 28 December.

import pandas as pd
import joblib

model = joblib.load("knn_smarket.joblib")    # the model File 1 saved, in the same folder
k = model.named_steps["kneighborsclassifier"].n_neighbors

# The new date: the returns of the two days before (in %)
new_day = pd.DataFrame({"Lag1": [-0.298], "Lag2": [0.130]})

prediction = model.predict(new_day)[0]
probabilities = model.predict_proba(new_day)[0]
print(f"Prediction for 30 December 2005: {prediction}")
for label, prob in zip(model.classes_, probabilities):
    print(f"   Pr({label}) = {prob:.3f}   "
          f"-> about {round(prob * k)} of the {k} nearest past days went {label}")
Prediction for 30 December 2005: Up
   Pr(Down) = 0.447   -> about 38 of the 85 nearest past days went Down
   Pr(Up) = 0.553   -> about 47 of the 85 nearest past days went Up

The probabilities are the votes of the \(K\) nearest past days, the \(\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i \in N_0} I(y_i = j)\) of the KNN rule. On 30 December 2005 the S&P 500 in fact fell 0.489%, so this prediction was wrong. One date proves nothing either way. File 1’s test year is how the model is judged; File 2 is how it is used.

Your turn: change the two numbers (for example Lag1 = 1.5, Lag2 = -0.8) and run File 2 again. Does a big rise yesterday change the vote?

What the financial example taught us

  1. Cross-validation chose \(K\) without touching the test year. It is the only honest way to tune a model, and it took five lines of code.
  2. With time series, the folds follow time. The past predicts the block that comes next, never the reverse.
  3. The test year judged once, and the verdict was “no signal”. A flexible method cannot create information that is not in the data. Knowing this before trading is worth a lot.
  4. Training and predicting are two different jobs. File 1 is done once, carefully. File 2 can then run every morning, on each new date, in a fraction of a second.

Swap the stock market for your own question: crisis or no crisis, a firm that exports or not, a country falling behind or not. The two files stay the same; only the data and the predictors change. That is what the practice asks you to do.

Big lessons from ML

Big lessons

  • Machine Learning is about:

    • regressions

    • classifications

  • Machine Learning is about:

    • a process: the 7 principles of ML (see the previous session)

  • You can run the regressions of sessions 2–6 — smf.ols, smf.logit, panel models — in the context of ML: k-fold cross-validation, training/testing, predictions

  • ML aims at:

    • reducing the model and data biases in sampling with regards to the populations

    • as such, it is a GIGANTIC improvement of current quantitative studies

Beyond one classifier

  • Classification: iris
  • Regression: house prices
  • A random forest
# Data with a real signal: three iris species from four flower measurements.
# The data ships with scikit-learn, so there is nothing to download.
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
iris_search = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier()),
                           {"kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors": range(1, 16)}, cv=10)
iris_search.fit(iris.data, iris.target)

print("best K:", iris_search.best_params_["kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors"])
print(f"CV accuracy: {iris_search.best_score_:.3f}")
best K: 8
CV accuracy: 0.967
# KNN can predict a number too: the average of the K nearest houses' prices.
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

URL = "https://www.warin.ca/datalake/courses_data/qmibr/session5/Real_Estate_Sample.csv"
houses = pd.read_csv(URL, index_col=0).dropna()
X = houses[["Living.area", "bedrooms", "bathrooms", "year", "garage"]]
y = houses["Price"]

models = {
    "KNN, K = 5": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=5)),
    "KNN, K = 25": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=25)),
    "linear regression": LinearRegression(),
}
for name, model in models.items():
    # scikit-learn returns NEGATIVE errors (it always maximises); the minus undoes it
    rmse = -cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error").mean()
    print(f"{name:18}  RMSE = {rmse:10,.0f}")
print(f"price standard deviation = {y.std():,.0f}   <- the cost of predicting the average")
KNN, K = 5          RMSE =    273,663
KNN, K = 25         RMSE =    259,959
linear regression   RMSE =    263,558
price standard deviation = 288,540   <- the cost of predicting the average
# Continues from File 1 (session08_1_train.py): X_train, y_train, search, majority.
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

# 500 trees, on every core of the machine (n_jobs=-1)
forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, n_jobs=-1, random_state=0)
forest_accuracy = cross_val_score(forest, X_train, y_train, cv=5).mean()

print(f"random forest CV accuracy = {forest_accuracy:.3f}")
print(f"KNN CV accuracy           = {search.best_score_:.3f}")
print(f"commonest class           = {majority:.3f}")
random forest CV accuracy = 0.495
KNN CV accuracy           = 0.525
commonest class           = 0.508

Five hundred trees, every core busy, and nothing beats the constant rule by much. The lesson is not about the method: these two lags may carry no signal, and no amount of compute manufactures one.
